First 13418 characters: Design and Stability of Load-Side Primary Frequency Control in Power Systems
abstract: We present a systematic method to design ubiquitous continuous fast-acting distributed load control for primary frequency regulation in power networks, by formulating an optimal load control (OLC) problem where the objective is to minimize the aggregate cost of tracking an operating point subject to power balance over the network. We prove that the swing dynamics and the branch power flows, coupled with frequency-based load control, serve as a distributed primal-dual algorithm to solve OLC. We establish the global asymptotic stability of a multimachine network under such type of load-side primary frequency control. These results imply that the local frequency deviations at each bus convey exactly the right information about the global power imbalance for the loads to make individual decisions that turn out to be globally optimal. Simulations confirm that the proposed algorithm can rebalance power and resynchronize bus frequencies after a disturbance with significantly improved transient performance.
Motivation: Frequency control maintains the frequency of a power system tightly around its nominal value when demand or supply fluctuates. It is traditionally implemented on the generation side and consists of three mechanisms that work at different timescales in concert , , . The primary frequency control operates at a timescale up to low tens of seconds and uses a governor to adjust, around a setpoint, the mechanical power input to a generator based on the local frequency deviation. It is called the droop control and is completely decentralized. The primary control can rebalance power and stabilize the frequency but does not in itself restore the nominal frequency. The secondary frequency control (called automatic generation control) operates at a timescale up to a minute or so and adjusts the setpoints of governors in a control area in a centralized fashion to drive the frequency back to its nominal value and the inter-area power flows to their scheduled values. Economic dispatch operates at a timescale of several minutes or up and schedules the output levels of generators that are online and the inter-area power flows. See for a recent hierarchical model of these three mechanisms and its stability analysis. This paper focuses on load participation in the primary frequency control.The needs and technologies for ubiquitous continuous fast-acting distributed load participation in frequency control at different timescales have started to mature in the last decade or so. The idea however dates back to the late 1970s. Schweppe et al. advocate its deployment to “assist or even replace turbine-governed systems and spinning reserve” . They also propose to use spot prices to incentivize the users to adapt their consumption to the true cost of generation at the time of consumption. Remarkably it was emphasized back then that such frequency adaptive loads will “allow the system to accept more readily a stochastically fluctuating energy source, such as wind or solar generation” . This point is echoed recently in, e.g., , , , , , , , that argue for “grid-friendly” appliances, such as refrigerators, water or space heaters, ventilation systems, and air conditioners, as well as plug-in electric vehicles to help manage energy imbalance. For further references, see . Simulations in all these studies have consistently shown significant improvement in performance and reduction in the need for spinning reserves. The benefit of this approach can thus be substantial as the total capacity of grid-friendly appliances in the U.S. is estimated in to be about 18% of the peak demand, comparable to the required operating reserve, currently at 13% of the peak demand. The feasibility of this approach is confirmed by experiments reported in that measured the correlation between the frequency at a 230kV transmission substation and the frequencies at the 120V wall outlets at various places in a city in Montana. They show that local frequency measurements are adequate for loads to participate in primary frequency control as well as in the damping of electromechanical oscillations due to inter-area modes of large interconnected systems.Indeed a small scale demonstration project has been conducted by the Pacific Northwest National Lab during early 2006 to March 2007 where 200 residential appliances participated in primary frequency control by automatically reducing their consumption (e.g, the heating element of a clothes dryer was turned off while the tumble continued) when the frequency of the household dropped below a threshold (59.95Hz) . Field trials are also carried out in other countries around the globe, e.g., the U.K. Market Transformation Program . Even though loads do not yet provide second-by-second or minute-by-minute continuous regulation service in any major electricity markets, the survey in finds that they already provide 50% of the 2,400 MW contingency reserve in ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas) and 30% of dispatched reserve energy (in between continuous reserve and economic dispatch) in the U.K. market. Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) developed LIPA Edge that provides 24.9 MW of demand reduction and 75 MW of spinning reserve by 23,400 loads for peak power management .While there are many simulation studies and field trials of frequency adaptive load control as discussed above, there is not much analytic study that relates the behavior of the loads and the equilibrium and dynamic behavior of a multimachine power network. Indeed this has been recognized, e.g., in , , , as a major unanswered question that must be resolved before ubiquitous continuous fast-acting distributed load participation in frequency regulation will become widespread. Even though classical models for power system dynamics , , that focus on the generator control can be adapted to include load adaptation, they do not consider the cost, or disutility, to the load in participating in primary frequency control, an important aspect of such an approach , , , .In this paper we present a systematic method to design ubiquitous continuous fast-acting distributed load control and establish the global asymptotic stability of a multimachine network under this type of primary frequency control. Our approach allows the loads to choose their consumption pattern based on their need and the global power imbalance on the network, attaining with the generation what calls a homeostatic equilibrium “to the benefit of both the utilities and their customers.” To the best of our knowledge, this is the first network model and analysis of load-side primary frequency control.
Summary: Specifically we consider a simple network model described by linearized swing dynamics at generator buses, power flow dynamics on the branches, and a measure of disutility to users when they participate in primary frequency control. At steady state, the frequencies at different buses are synchronized to a common nominal value and the mechanic power is balanced with the electric power at each bus. Suppose a small change in power injection occurs on an arbitrary subset of the buses, causing the bus frequencies to deviate from their nominal value. We assume the change is small and the DC power flow model is reasonably accurate. Instead of adjusting the generators as in the traditional approach, how should we adjust the controllable loads in the network to rebalance power in a way that minimizes the aggregate disutility of these loads? We formulate this question as an optimal load control (OLC) problem, which informally takes the form rCld c(d) subject to power rebalance where {{formula:a310fe84-e45f-42cf-a732-95a0b3e16a81}} is the demand vector and {{formula:f4f39df7-1a11-4bb0-b9f6-c1142a32ce69}} measures the disutility to loads in participating in control. Even though neither frequency nor branch power flows appear in OLC, we will show that frequency deviations emerge as a measure of the cost of power imbalance and branch flow deviations as a measure of frequency asynchronism. More strikingly the swing dynamics together with local frequency-based load control serve as a distributed primal-dual algorithm to solve the dual of OLC. This primal-dual algorithm is globally asymptotically stable, steering the network to the unique global optimal of OLC.These results have four important implications. First the local frequency deviation at each bus conveys exactly the right information about the global power imbalance for the loads themselves to make local decisions that turn out to be globally optimal. This allows a completely decentralized solution without explicit communication to or among the loads. Second the global asymptotic stability of the primal-dual algorithm of OLC suggests that ubiquitous continuous decentralized load participation in primary frequency control is stable, addressing a question raised in several prior studies, e.g. , , , . Third we present a “forward engineering” perspective where we start with the basic goal of load control and derive the frequency-based controller and the swing dynamics as a distributed primal-dual algorithm to solve the dual of OLC. In this perspective the controller design mainly boils down to specifying an appropriate optimization problem (OLC). Fourth the opposite perspective of “reverse engineering” is useful as well where, given an appropriate frequency-based controller design, the network dynamics will converge to a unique equilibrium that inevitably solves OLC with an objective function that depends on the controller design. In this sense any frequency adaptation implies a certain disutility function of the load that the control implicitly minimizes. For instance the linear controller in , implies a quadratic disutility function and hence a quadratic objective in OLC.Our results confirm that frequency adaptive loads can rebalance power and resynchronize frequency, just as the droop control of the generators currently does. They fit well with the emerging layered control architecture advocated in .
Our prior work and structure of paper: In our previous papers , , we consider a power network that is tightly coupled electrically and can be modeled as a single generator connected to a group of loads. A disturbance in generation causes the (single) frequency to deviate from its nominal value. The goal is to adapt loads, using local frequency measurements in the presence of additive noise, to rebalance power at minimum disutility. The model for generator dynamics in is more detailed than the model in this paper. Here we study a network of generator and load buses with branch flows between them and their local frequencies during transient. We use a simpler model for individual generators and focus on the effect of the network structure on frequency-based load control.The paper is organized as follows. Section describes a dynamic model of power networks. Section formulates OLC as a systematic method to design load-side primary frequency control and explains how the frequency-based load control and the system dynamics serve as a distributed primal-dual algorithm to solve OLC. Section proves that the network equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable. Section reports simulations of the IEEE 68-bus test system that uses a much more detailed and realistic model than our analytic model. The simulation results not only confirm the convergence of the primal-dual algorithm, but also demonstrate significantly better transient performance. Section concludes the paper.

Conclusion: We have presented a systematic method to design ubiquitous continuous fast-acting distributed load control for primary frequency regulation in power networks, by formulating an optimal load control (OLC) problem where the objective is to minimize the aggregate control cost subject to power balance across the network. We have shown that the dynamics of generator swings and the branch power flows, coupled with a frequency-based load control, serve as a distributed primal-dual algorithm to solve the dual problem of OLC. Even though the system has multiple equilibrium points with nonunique branch power flows, we have proved that it nonetheless converges to a unique optimal point. Simulation of the IEEE 68-bus test system confirmed that the proposed mechanism can rebalance power and resynchronize bus frequencies with significantly improved transient performance.
Simulation showing feature of model: A key assumption underlying the analytic model ()–() is that different buses may have their own frequencies during transient, instead of resynchronizing almost instantaneously to a common system frequency which then converges to an equilibrium. Simulation of the 68-bus test system confirms this phenomenon. Fig. REF shows all the 68 bus frequencies from the simulation with the same step change {{formula:7720452a-f0f8-4ff8-8a51-1f99bb86ed36}} as that in Section but without OLC. First 12974 characters: Fragility of Decentralized Load-Side Frequency Control in Stochastic Environment
abstract: In this paper, we demonstrate the fragility of decentralized load-side frequency algorithms proposed in [1] against stochastic parametric uncertainty in power network model. The stochastic parametric uncertainty is motivated through the presence of renewable energy resources in power system model. We show that relatively small variance value of the parametric uncertainty affecting the system bus voltages cause the decentralized load-side frequency regulation algorithm to become stochastically unstable. The critical variance value of the stochastic bus voltages above which the decentralized control algorithm become mean square unstable is computed using an analytical framework developed in [2], [3]. Furthermore, the critical variance value is shown to decrease with the increase in the cost of the controllable loads and with the increase in penetration of renewable energy resources. Finally, simulation results on IEEE 68 bus system are presented to verify the main findings of the paper.
Introduction: In this paper, we show that the decentralized load-side frequency control algorithm proposed in is very fragile to parametric uncertainty in power network model. One of the essential components of the smart grid vision is the active participation of loads for improved operation and performance of network power system at different time scales . The technology is maturing to the point where the smart grid vision can be realized for actively controlling the loads to absorb not only the long-term variability or uncertainty from renewable power generation but also short term fluctuations. The application of load-side control for frequency regulation falls into the latter category. With the potential benefits of active load control, there are increased research efforts towards the development of systematic analytical methods and optimization-based tools for distributed load control. Most of the literature on this topic primarily focus on stability properties of control algorithms developed for load-side frequency regulation , , , , , . In particular, proves the asymptotic stability of primal-dual gradient system leading to the decentralized algorithm for load-side frequency control. However, the important issue related to the performance of these algorithms is not addressed primarily in the presence of parametric uncertainty in power network model.For the successful implementation of the various developed algorithms, it is important to analyze the performance of these algorithms against both parametric and additive sources of uncertainties. In this paper, we extended the primal-dual gradient system model of power swing equation with controllable loads developed in to incorporate the stochastic parametric uncertainty. There are various sources of parametric uncertainty in power system model. In this paper, we argue that renewable energy resources in the form of wind and solar are the potential source of parametric uncertainty in the network power system, where stochasticity in the availability of renewable energy resources will lead to stochastic bus voltages. We develop stochastic power network model with the additive as well as the multiplicative source of uncertainty. The stochastic notion of mean square stability is used to analyze the stability of network power system using stochastic stability framework for the continuous-time system developed in , , . The continuous-time stochastic stability framework discussed in this paper is motivated from stochastic stability analysis and control results developed for linear and nonlinear systems in , , , . The developed framework is used to determine the critical variance, {{formula:74783872-2f4e-485f-b4a7-900d635fdf63}} , of parametric stochastic uncertainty above which, the system is mean square unstable. We show that decentralized load-side frequency regulation algorithm developed in is extremely fragile to stochastic fluctuations in bus voltages. In particular, we show that, with an increase in the cost of the controllable loads, the value of critical variance, {{formula:a4866505-0e53-4ef8-9094-0c80ee677c2b}} , above which the system is unstable decreases. Furthermore, {{formula:a38687af-05c9-4241-83ff-caeff4a2d8cf}} value also decreases with the increase in the penetration of the renewable energy resources in the power network.The organization of the paper is as follows. In section , we provide a framework for incorporating stochastic parametric uncertainty in dynamic power system model employed for solving the load-side frequency regulation problem. Results on analyzing the mean square stability of stochastic power network model are discussed in section . Simulation results on IEEE 68 bus system are presented in section followed by conclusion in section .
Load-side frequency control model with stochasticity: In this section, we develop an integrated load-side frequency control model with stochastic uncertainty. There are various sources of stochastic uncertainty in a power network and renewables energy sources such as solar and wind energy forms the major contributors to the uncertainty. We first discuss briefly the deterministic load-side frequency control model as developed in . We refer the readers to for more detailed discussion on this model. The basic idea behind the load-side frequency control is to control the loads, so that, the system-wide frequency can be regulated following a small change in power injection at one of the system bus. The load control comes at a cost and is measured by the aggregate disutility of the loads. The objective is to regulate the system frequency while minimizing the aggregate disutility of the loads.To set up the problem, consider a power network as a graph network with generator and load buses as nodes and transmission lines as edges. Let the sets {{formula:39815f7c-c2d9-4b4b-8733-b497ca429f63}} , and {{formula:cacfc9de-b398-4345-8fbc-1224f234f72f}} respectively, denote the set of generator nodes, set of load nodes, and the set containing network edges. The cardinalities of the sets {{formula:d1a4c09f-8cc7-47dc-b7ab-4943a6584548}} , and {{formula:48cb3aab-0f03-4316-9beb-eda66a551692}} are denoted by {{formula:0507fb6e-41c9-45fe-984b-7bd24c579e8c}} , and {{formula:9ac2c28f-239d-4e10-a4f4-4d828a2a9dc2}} respectively. Let {{formula:73ccbed8-7d4c-4b85-a955-91fb89c98f10}} denote the set of generator and load nodes and its cardinality is given by {{formula:f1bc1b68-9e40-4307-9306-c908298a4ec1}} , where {{formula:f8c06530-db61-4192-9852-d83e57d40eaa}} . Stochastic Renewables and Parametric Uncertainty: In this subsection, we show how the parametric uncertainty enters in the power system dynamics. We motivate the parametric uncertainty in the power system dynamics through the presence of renewables where the intermittent nature of wind and solar energy resources are modeled as stochastic random variables. The network power system with parametric uncertainty can be modeled as a set of differential algebraic equations (DAEs) written as follows: {{formula:cb206871-ba80-4e07-993d-6a455df62ecc}}where, {{formula:a2c3e62e-a9bb-433d-b22a-9819df5b44a7}} are the dynamic states corresponding to generator angular velocities, generator excitation voltages, power across the transmission lines, etc., and {{formula:ee5aed25-64ef-4379-b52e-576ca27972c1}} are the network as well as generator algebraic states corresponding to the bus voltages, bus angles, currents, etc. and {{formula:8ef806d7-b671-4a8e-8535-67d76546f659}} denotes the stochastic parametric uncertainty. Conclusion: We showed that the decentralized load-side frequency regulation algorithm is fragile to stochastic parametric uncertainty in a power network. The presence of stochastic uncertainty is motivated through uncertainty in renewables. (3) The stochastic model is expressed as a feedback interconnection of a deterministic stable system with multiplicative stochastic uncertainty (equations and description of the feedback form). (4) Mean‑square (second‑moment) stability is defined and a necessary and sufficient condition for mean‑square exponential stability is given (Theorem 6). (6) It explicitly reports that even a relatively small variance makes the algorithm “stochastically unstable” and that the critical variance decreases when (a) the cost coefficient of controllable loads increases and (b) the penetration level of renewables increases (abstract, results section). (7) Simulation results on the IEEE‑68 bus system illustrate frequencies growing unbounded when the variance exceeds the critical value, confirming loss of stability. All these steps are directly quoted or paraphrased from the provided text, so the effect of stochastic bus‑voltage uncertainty on the stability of the originally deterministic, asymptotically stable algorithm is fully supported.

experimenterPromptBothResult.explanation: The first paper establishes that the decentralized load‑side frequency control algorithm is globally asymptotically stable when the power network is modeled deterministically (swing dynamics, branch flows, and frequency‑based load control). The second paper explicitly extends this model to include stochastic parametric uncertainty in the bus voltages (motivated by renewable generation). It shows: (1) the stochastic model can be written as a feedback interconnection of the deterministic stable system and a multiplicative uncertainty; (2) mean‑square (second‑moment) stability of the overall system requires the deterministic part to be Hurwitz, but the presence of voltage uncertainty can violate this condition; (3) a critical variance of the stochastic voltage fluctuations is derived, above which the system becomes mean‑square unstable, i.e., frequencies grow unbounded despite the deterministic asymptotic stability; (4) the critical variance decreases with higher controllable‑load cost and with greater renewable penetration, confirming the algorithm’s fragility. These statements directly answer how stochastic voltage uncertainty degrades the original deterministic stability, turning asymptotic stability into potential mean‑square instability and defining a variance threshold that must not be exceeded.

First 12500 characters: Imprecise Monte Carlo simulation and iterative importance sampling for the estimation of lower previsions
abstract: We develop a theoretical framework for studying numerical estimation of lower previsions, generally applicable to two-level Monte Carlo methods, importance sampling methods, and a wide range of other sampling methods one might devise. We link consistency of these estimators to Glivenko-Cantelli classes, and for the sub-Gaussian case we show how the correlation structure of this process can be used to bound the bias and prove consistency. We also propose a new upper estimator, which can be used along with the standard lower estimator, in order to provide a simple confidence interval. As a case study of this framework, we then discuss how importance sampling can be exploited to provide accurate numerical estimates of lower previsions. We propose an iterative importance sampling method to drastically improve the performance of imprecise importance sampling. We demonstrate our results on the imprecise Dirichlet model.
Introduction: Various sensible approaches to sampling for estimation of lower previsions can be found in the literature. A case study comparing a wide range of techniques, specifically aimed at reliability analysis, can be found in .A first approach is to use two-level Monte Carlo sampling, where first one samples distributions over the (extreme points of the) credal set, and then samples from these distributions, In the context of belief functions, one can also sample random sets, and then evaluate the resulting belief function through optimisation over these sets . A third more sophisticated approach comprises of importance sampling from a reference distribution, and then solve an optimisation problem over the importance sampling weights , , .Two-level Monte Carlo can be rather inefficient, especially if a credal set is high-dimensional or if it has a large number of extreme points. Moreover, two-level Monte Carlo generally only provides a non-conservative solution.Random set sampling is more efficient, but requires a large number of optimisation problems to be solved (one for each sample), and requires a suitable belief function approximation to be identified if one wants to apply this to arbitrary lower previsions.Importance sampling in imprecise probability has been studied already in the '90s; see for example , , for some early works. Importance sampling can be quite effective. For example, have successfully used sensitivity analysis over importance sampling weights with respect to the mean parameter of a normal distribution. In , importance sampling is used over both the mean and the variance parameters of a normal distribution using a 2-dimensional grid. A common issue with importance sampling is that estimates can be very poor if the reference distribution is far off the optimal distribution. This has been recently addressed in , where an iterative self-normalised importance sampling method is proposed that requires far less computational power compared to standard importance sampling methods for sensitivity analysis, in the sense that far smaller samples can be used, and that far smaller optimisation problems need to be solved. A very similar approach using standard importance sampling was proposed in .A second issue, which has received little attention in the literature, concerns the bias and consistency of these estimates. Two-level Monte Carlo methods and importance sampling methods are essentially constructed as lower envelopes of estimators for precise expectations. To the best of the author's knowledge, in the context of imprecise probability, the bias and consistency of such lower envelopes has not yet been studied elsewhere in the literature.The first purpose of this paper is to develop a theoretical framework for studying numerical estimation of lower previsions. We do so by looking, in essence, at the estimation of the minimum of an unknown function, given that we can `simulate' the function to an arbitrary degree of precision. This framework applies to two-level Monte Carlo methods, importance sampling methods, and a wide range of other sampling methods one might devise. A first contribution of this paper is a link between consistency of such envelopes and a Glivenko-Cantelli class condition. In case our estimators can be described by a sub-Gaussian process (by the central limit theorem, this will often hold if the sample size is taken large enough), we show how the correlation structure of this process can be used to bound the bias. We provide sufficient conditions for consistency, and we also identify situations where consistency fails. We rely heavily on stochastic process theory, and in particular, on Talagrand's results on the supremum of stochastic processes .Although we obtain theoretical bounds, these bounds are not practical in the sense that they require us to bound a rather tricky functional. A second theoretical contribution of the paper is that we propose a new `upper' estimator, which can be used along with the standard lower envelope estimator, in order to provide a single comprehensive confidence interval. Unfortunately, the consistency of this upper estimator is still an open problem, although it is guaranteed to provide an upper bound (hence its name). However, we can identify one situation under which the upper estimator is unbiased.A second aim of the paper is to study importance sampling for the estimation of lower previsions. We follow , , , and look specifically at how we can take envelopes over the importance sampling weights directly in order to obtain sampling estimates, without needing to draw large numbers of samples, and without needing to solve large numbers of optimisation problems. Unlike , however, we do not just look at Bayesian sensitivity analysis, and admit arbitrary sets of distributions in our theoretical treatment. Also unlike for instance , , , , , in this paper, we use self-normalised importance sampling instead of standard importance sampling, as it is known that this drastically speeds up calculations . In this paper, we will also show that it ensures coherence of the resulting estimates (regardless of bias).We then revisit the iterative importance sampling method proposed in , . The key novelty of this method is the idea of iteratively changing the importance sampling distribution itself, in order to ensure that the final answer has an effective sample size that is as close as possible to the actual sample size. In this paper, we focus on obtaining proper confidence intervals. We reconfirm that the iterative method requires far less computational power compared to standard importance sampling methods for sensitivity analysis, in the sense that far smaller samples can be used, and that far smaller optimisation problems need to be solved. We also identify conditions under which we can obtain confidence intervals almost instantly.The paper is structured as follows. In sec:estimation, we study the theory behind lower envelopes of estimators. We study bias, consistency, and two ways to obtain a confidence interval. In sec:iteratedimpsamp, we study importance sampling for the estimation of lower previsions. We briefly review the basic theory, and then we revisit the iterative importance sampling method proposed in , , from the perspective of the results derived in the preceding section. Some numerical examples demonstrate our approach, using the imprecise Dirichlet model. We conclude in sec:conclusion.
Imprecise Estimation: The aim of this section is to provide a general theoretical framework for studying the lower envelope of a parameterized set of estimators. The main idea is that we can use such a lower envelope to estimate the minimum of an unknown (or, hard to evaluate) function. The application that we have in mind is one where we have a parameterized set of estimators for the expectation of some quantity, and we wish to estimate the lower expectation. However, the theory developed in this section is not tied to any specific parameterized set of estimators.

Conclusion: We developed a theoretical framework for estimating the minimum of an unknown function, given an estimator for that function. This allowed us then to study estimation of lower previsions. For estimators that have the form of a sample mean, we identified the Glivenko-Cantelli condition as a sufficient condition for consistency, and we bounded the bias in the sub-Gaussian case by means of Talagrand's functional, and identified when consistency fails.The theoretical bounds, based on Talagrand's functional, are not practical in the sense that there is no quick and easy way to evaluate them analytically. Therefore, we proposed a new `upper' estimator, which can be used along with the standard lower envelope estimator. This allowed us to construct a practical confidence interval. Unfortunately, we could not say much about the consistency of this upper estimator, and our numerical experiments confirmed that this estimator may not perform too well in practice: in some of our importance sampling examples, the upper bound estimate was far more conservative than the lower bound. However, we identified one situation under which the upper estimator is unbiased: this is precisely when the lower bound provides `stable' estimates, in the sense that we described.As a specific application of this theoretical framework, we then described how envelopes of importance sampling estimates can be used to estimate lower previsions. The key observation that makes this possible is that importance sampling allows us to estimate means not just from the distribution that we are sampling from, but from an entire neighbourhood of distributions around the sampling distribution. Through straightforward optimisation over the importance sampling weights, we can therefore estimate lower previsions without having to, say, draw samples from all extreme points of the credal set. This technique is simple and is readily applicable for medium sized problems.We saw that, especially in higher dimensions, taking envelopes over the weights may not work very well, due to poor effective sample sizes especially when the optimal distribution is far away from the sampling distribution. We revisited the iterative procedure proposed in , , which naturally moves the sampling distribution towards the optimal distribution. We demonstrated how this led to a much quicker estimate with far less computational power required. In this paper, we also studied the confidence intervals that arise from this method, and we saw that we can compute them very quickly, at least if the procedure is `stable' in a specific sense.Whilst the procedure that we have described will work well for medium sized problems, we foresee that for really large scale problems, the effective sample size may still be too limited to ensure that the optimal distribution can be identified at all. In such cases, perhaps the credal set could scale throughout the algorithm, in order to ensure a reasonable effective sample size, and therefore to help convergence of the algorithm.Another idea is to use importance sampling to explore only a very small region of the credal set, but then to use the resulting derivative information to move the sampling distribution in the right direction. A problem with this however is that the derivatives obtained are quite noisy, and in practice we have not found a good way of using these noisy derivatives to ensure convergence.Despite the many open questions listed in sec:openquestions, iterative importance sampling for lower previsions seems promising. Even if we cannot answer the above questions yet, we can obtain accurate confidence intervals for envelopes of more or less arbitrary parameterized sets of densities and arbitrary gambles. We are thus, in principle, no longer restricted to specific gambles or dependent on conjugacy or other special analytical properties of our credal set in order to work with lower previsions.Finally, we emphasize once more that the results from sec:estimation are not just applicable to the estimation of lower previsions, but to arbitrary envelopes of sets of estimators. This might potentially be useful in other fields, for instance for the optimisation of functions approximated by an emulator, provided the emulator is sub-Gaussian.

First 12500 characters: Monte Carlo Estimation for Imprecise Probabilities: Basic Properties
abstract: We describe Monte Carlo methods for estimating lower envelopes of expectations of real random variables. We prove that the estimation bias is negative and that its absolute value shrinks with increasing sample size. We discuss fairly practical techniques for proving strong consistency of the estimators and use these to prove the consistency of an example in the literature. We also provide an example where there is no consistency.
Introduction: Monte Carlo simulation is a technique widely used for obtaining numerical estimates for in principle anything that can be represented as a sum or an integral. Multiple research fields have proposed to extend the Monte Carlo method towards solving optimisation problems. Both the fields of stochastic optimisation and empirical processes have for example studied the properties of such generalised Monte Carlo estimators, including their bias , their consistency and a version of the central limit theorem , for them. In the field of imprecise probabilities, Monte Carlo based methods have also received considerable attention , , , , , , , , but with the exception of the discussion in , the theoretical properties of the corresponding estimators have not been investigated in much detail. We here address this by studying the bias and consistency of a large class of imprecise Monte-Carlo based estimators, including the important special case of imprecise Monte-Carlo estimators that are based on importance sampling , , , .The optimisation or extremum problem we typically encounter in the imprecise probabilities field is calculating the lower expectation {{formula:406d0dad-ef11-4370-b259-544397b565a6}} —or the upper expectation {{formula:0474b013-9681-4e86-85fd-ccfe653cb072}} —of a Borel measurable map {{formula:1d4772de-10cf-49e1-90d1-7e46c45dab88}} of a real random variable {{formula:4363de17-44d8-4a8b-881d-59ee4b210f19}} , whose distribution {{formula:256bfa14-d21b-4dd1-9562-1152771e3005}} is only known to belong to a set {{formula:a2314669-a7e6-4594-a03d-bd382d842015}} .More generally, {{formula:63b01740-55ff-482e-82ea-b620fa831ef9}} could be a real random vector, and {{formula:bcfacc29-88af-489c-a809-84b75b0f79a1}} a vector-valued map, but we will only consider the scalar case here. To find this lower expectation {{formula:64b09a40-a503-4cc7-b4a0-94ad5dbc115f}}we have to minimise the expected value {{formula:93368242-7cdf-466c-ae45-691234702dce}} —a sum or an integral that would typically be estimated using Monte Carlo simulation—over a set of distributions {{formula:15437445-0d1a-4c85-b4d0-5e5166ee3ab0}} . A fairly straightforward—but naive—method for estimating this infimum consists in choosing a finite subset {{formula:b5e5f5d9-6482-4e1c-95c8-67b28f509820}} of {{formula:b3c644b0-10a3-44fb-b4fe-da3ee706d71a}} , taking independent samples for each probability measure {{formula:524c8be4-8b07-4c19-baa0-bb74e1be54f7}} , using them to get to a Monte Carlo estimate for {{formula:6dc8acbb-5d63-4e98-9df9-a83e3a4f18b4}} , and finally finding the minimum of the Monte Carlo estimates. The problem with this method is that the larger the set of probabilities {{formula:358bee92-377e-4935-b2af-e11c85ccf665}} , the larger the bias it will tend to produce, as we argue in Section REF .To reduce this bias, we would typically want to introduce correlation between the estimates of {{formula:9ced10db-73dd-455b-b360-f062e6be4117}} for different {{formula:58c319a9-128a-45dc-ad7f-98c917241793}} . One way to do this is to sample from a single distribution only, and to use these samples to calculate the corresponding samples for the distributions in the set {{formula:e19d157e-e9dc-4f6c-8c99-4bb689c8bcf2}} . We will therefore in this paper study estimators of the form {{formula:d6bdccc6-1577-452a-a6e0-290eaffd0327}}where we take independent samples {{formula:87f65505-fe51-41ba-9b5b-240b6b43e812}} from a single distribution {{formula:f34c757e-6ad9-42c7-a41f-ae97cfe83439}} and transform the results into samples for other distributions, parametrised by a set {{formula:3b9049a8-f632-4fa3-8b32-f262790cd882}} —this transformation, as we shall see further on, accounts for the use of the maps {{formula:7ce1377b-d448-4d95-9716-ab20264b6cc0}} rather than the map {{formula:41499860-559c-4fa9-9fbe-272334292446}} in the estimator (REF ). A word on terminology is in order here. We will be careful in this paper to distinguish between functions and maps on some domain; maps are always defined on all of the domain, whereas functions may, but need not be, defined only on a part of the domain.The decomposition of the problem into a classical random variable {{formula:9b9a146b-b8b0-4489-a612-f9721b3682f3}} and a parametric part {{formula:0819eaa2-34cf-4c5c-ac5f-1959224c90f4}} is essential for our results, and is also present in the literature , . We show how to prove consistency for this fairly general type of estimators, and we give sufficient conditions for consistency that are relatively easy to check.The plan of the paper is as follows. First, in Section , we describe the theoretical setting of the discussion, and explain in some detail why we use estimators of the general form (REF ). We discuss two particular methods for generating samples of sufficient generality, where the resulting estimator has this general form. In Section we study a number of statistical properties of estimators of type (REF ): their bias and consistency. To show that the results we derive are practically useful, we include a discussion of two examples, in Section . In the first example, we show how to actually prove the consistency of an estimator encountered in the literature . The second example is a case where there is no consistency, provably. In the Conclusion, we highlight our main findings, and provide pointers to future work.extendedversion In order not to interrupt the flow of the discussion too much, we have moved all proofs to the Appendix. Proofs of our results are available in an extended arXiv version .
Notation and Theoretical Setting: Let us begin by sketching the theoretical background, and fixing the basic notation.We consider the measurable space {{formula:2cea369f-c344-404f-b87c-b71c521ab5f3}} , where {{formula:44dc50ac-e0c9-40ce-a384-0df18f39f1e2}} is the Borel {{formula:58b38c7f-492b-47cb-8000-aa17df984fc5}} -field on the set {{formula:6bfc54e7-64bc-420a-a71c-0f43ecdb30b3}} of all reals. We now identify the countable infinity of real random variables {{formula:4c2694ed-604c-4d78-838e-947b5aaf2f1c}} on {{formula:fabc5a75-0a59-4329-9b5a-567f8fe082c6}} , each of which is the projection map from the Cartesian product {{formula:0d275f61-34a2-4183-88ed-c4da420ef042}} to its {{formula:0b370827-440d-4939-94a1-e089ea7348be}} -th component space {{formula:66e061f3-272a-4f89-b7a9-0633e77891c7}} . reasoning.step1: The Tait-Kneser theorem (from paper math/0602317) states that osculating circles of a smooth plane curve free from vertices are pairwise disjoint, meaning they do not intersect and form a non-differentiable foliation.
reasoning.step2: In paper 1605.02117, the evolute of a plane curve is defined as the locus of centers of its osculating circles, and it is shown that this evolute corresponds to a null curve in Minkowski 3-space via the isotropic projection of Laguerre geometry.
reasoning.connectionExplanation: The disjointness of osculating circles from step 1 ensures that the family of osculating circles is a foliation without intersections, which implies that the evolute (the curve formed by their centers) is a regular curve. In the Minkowski 3-space representation, this regular curve becomes a null curve, as described in step 2. Thus, step 2 depends on step 1 because the property of being pairwise disjoint guarantees that the evolute is well-defined and can be mapped to a null curve.

question: What is the geometric relationship between the pairwise disjointness of osculating circles of a plane curve and the nature of its evolute in Minkowski 3-space?
answerWithPaperReferences: The Tait-Kneser theorem from [Paper A] ensures that osculating circles of a smooth plane curve without vertices are pairwise disjoint, forming a non-differentiable foliation. This disjointness implies that the evolute—the locus of centers of these osculating circles—is a regular curve. In [Paper B], the evolute is shown to correspond to a null curve in Minkowski 3-space via the isotropic projection in Laguerre geometry. Therefore, the pairwise disjointness of osculating circles underlies the existence of the evolute as a null curve.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: The osculating circles of a smooth plane curve without vertices do not intersect, which means they form a foliation. The evolute, which is the curve traced by the centers of these osculating circles, is therefore regular. In the context of Minkowski 3-space, this evolute appears as a null curve, reflecting the geometric relationship between the disjoint circles and their envelope.
isNotSingleHop: This question is not single-hop because it requires combining two distinct pieces of information: first, the property of osculating circles being pairwise disjoint from the Tait-Kneser theorem, and second, the representation of the evolute as a null curve in Minkowski 3-space. Neither piece alone answers the question; the connection between them requires reasoning across both papers.

First 12500 characters: Variations on the Tait-Kneser theorem
abstract: The classical Tait-Kneser theorem states that the osculating circles of a smooth plane curve, free from curvature extrema, are pairwise disjoint. We prove a number of analogs of this theorem, e.g., for ovals of osculating cubics, osculating polynomials and trigonometric polynomials; in each case, we will obtain a non-differentiable foliation with smooth leaves.
Introduction: At every point, a smooth plane curve can be approximated, to second order, by a circle; this circle is called osculating. One may think of the osculating circle as passing through three infinitesimally close points of the curve. A vertex of the curve is a point at which the osculating circle hyper-osculates: it approximates the curve to third order. Equivalently, a vertex is a critical point of the curvature function.Consider a (necessarily non-closed) curve, free from vertices. The classical Tait-Kneser theorem , (see also , ), states that the osculating circles of the curve are pairwise disjoint, see Figure REF . This theorem is closely related to the four vertex theorem of S. Mukhopadhyaya that a plane oval has at least 4 vertices (see again , ). {{figure:bdf51c17-9d45-48d4-a485-75dafd3f3ec7}}Figure REF illustrates the Tait-Kneser theorem: it shows an annulus foliated by osculating circles of a curve.Remark 1.1 This foliation is not differentiable! Here is a proof. Let {{formula:fb3ff623-7518-4cae-ad1e-31ae6d96b318}} be a differentiable function in the annulus, constant on the leaves. We claim that {{formula:30b30a10-6fb7-4120-9f2c-3d95b8b4dc12}} is constant. Indeed, {{formula:63b85afa-ad8f-46dd-a96f-0b7ac2213662}} vanishes on the tangent vectors to the leaves. The curve is tangent to its osculating circle at every point, hence {{formula:8f0816e8-892c-46b9-8364-a40c06324f11}} vanishes on the curve as well. Hence {{formula:57358c0e-aaa3-4ed7-8d4e-771a6ef9ad9f}} is constant on the curve. But the curve intersects all the circles that form the annulus, so {{formula:997bd06c-931b-45ca-9899-85762e4f4783}} is constant everywhere.Remark 1.2 The Tait-Kneser theorem has an analog in plane Minkowski geometry, see .We will prove a number of analogs of the Tait-Kneser theorem; in each case, we will obtain a non-differentiable foliation with smooth leaves.

First 12500 characters: Evolutes of plane curves and null curves in Minkowski $3$-space
abstract: We use the isotropic projection of Laguerre geometry in order to establish a correspondence between plane curves and null curves in the Minkowski $3$-space. We describe the geometry of null curves (Cartan frame, pseudo-arc parameter, pseudo-torsion, pairs of associated curves) in terms of the curvature of the corresponding plane curves. This leads to an alternative description of all plane curves which are Laguerre congruent to a given one.
Introduction: Two dimensional Laguerre geometry is the geometry of oriented contact between circles in the Euclidean plane {{formula:23b5c0bc-df15-40f2-9ba3-8c59e2a6d076}} (points of {{formula:662746f3-1203-447f-8c32-c6a3476bad2f}} are viewed as circles with radius zero). An efficient and intuitive model of Laguerre geometry is the so called Minkowski model , . This model establishes a 1-1 correspondence, called the isotropic projection , , between points in the Minkowski 3-space {{formula:d15068ee-4d04-4c99-b745-4424c5f1d2e4}} and oriented circles in the Euclidean plane. The group of Laguerre transformations is identified with the subgroup of the group of affine transformations of {{formula:03a0993c-806b-4579-8a3e-c8a030ad47c8}} which is generated by linear (Lorentzian) isometries, translations and dilations of {{formula:152e6e60-4981-465d-a48f-902b3d819759}} .A differentiable one-parameter family of circles in the Euclidean plane corresponds, via isotropic projection, to a differentiable curve in the Minkowski 3-space. In particular, the family of osculating circles to a given plane curve {{formula:74389b8c-1f4d-4021-90d9-c313b9e2d7e1}} corresponds to a certain curve {{formula:422ad9da-694f-42b8-9fb2-d424ab2e4236}} in {{formula:4cf0d035-bd69-4a96-be58-b51233c645ad}} , which we will call the {{formula:4485bac1-9baf-409c-a7b8-d81446ce748d}} -evolute of {{formula:4a225c7b-a3b7-43e4-8f70-4c31a43579ff}} . The {{formula:b156ce53-7934-44c3-8383-0223c5c3abf2}} -evolute of a plane curve is a null curve and, conversely, any null curve is the {{formula:6d2e95bb-4292-4e69-8a28-d5631b61cf4f}} -evolute of some plane curve (see Section ).The importance of light like (degenerate) submanifolds in relativity theory has been emphasized by many mathematical and physical researchers (see the monographs , ). Several authors have also investigated the particular case of null curves in the Minkowski 3-space (see the surveys , ). In the present paper we describe the geometry of null curves (Cartan frame, pseudo-arc parameter, pseudo-torsion) in terms of the curvature of the corresponding plane curves. This leads us to the notion of potential function (see Definition REF ). A potential function together with an initial condition completely determines the null curve and the underlying plane curve through the formulae of Theorem REF . As a consequence, we obtain an alternative description of all plane curves which are Laguerre congruent to a given curve {{formula:fd76e50d-9780-4740-9310-9f81e3170036}} as follows (see Remark REF for details): starting with the plane curve {{formula:14b9e9a2-c144-453a-8735-88332f204544}} , compute the pseudo-torsion {{formula:428d52fd-ba76-40c3-bffd-91fa7a11cce3}} of its {{formula:61cb2513-de27-4b10-97fc-3bd65e2d27fd}} -evolute; up to scale, the pseudo-torsion is invariant under Laguerre transformations of {{formula:0d14d22c-402b-44cf-8c33-0752136bfb42}} and the potential functions associated to null curves with pseudo-torsion {{formula:19acff69-fb8d-4f6b-8be9-cb9b9ce199db}} are precisely the solutions of a certain second order differential equation; use formulae of Theorem REF to recover from these solutions the corresponding plane curves; in this way, we obtain all the plane curves which are Laguerre congruent with {{formula:5f1cae9c-a830-462a-9c9f-34cc3816aa8f}} .In Section , we describe, in terms of their potential functions, some classes of associated null curves: Bertrand pairs , , null curves with common binormal lines , and binormal-directional curves . We shall also prove the following two interesting results on null curves: 1) a null helix parameterized by pseudo-arc admits a null curve parameterized by pseudo-arc with common binormal lines at corresponding points if, and only if, it has pseudo-torsion {{formula:d48e3d0f-1163-48cf-ab05-0d865bb90fbd}} (see Corollary REF ); 2) given a null curve {{formula:c54dc2f8-a5fb-430d-962f-2484e86636e0}} parameterized by pseudo-arc, there exists a null helix {{formula:447f185d-b553-4ea0-ab2d-b559ee7453c2}} parameterized by pseudo-arc with constant pseudo-torsion {{formula:6b2edb6f-271e-4028-9a61-afabfed55371}} and a 1-1 correspondence between points of the two curves {{formula:a1a58429-f951-4917-b8f0-c294ed644630}} and {{formula:f13bf3c5-e2a8-40aa-aa41-30a11f52d7d4}} such that, at corresponding points, the tangent lines are parallel (see Theorem REF ).
Curves in the Euclidean plane: We start by fixing some notation and by recalling standard facts concerning curves in the Euclidean plane.Let {{formula:5a00e4fc-3455-4f83-a3bf-10cc579b3557}} be an open interval of {{formula:6c8dc6fc-55a9-46d6-a457-95c1fc8a8b67}} and {{formula:239de4a2-578e-4973-8532-ea103f34b69a}} be a regular plane curve, that is, {{formula:a6208f86-36a9-4340-8c2a-a2fcb09ee24b}} is differentiable sufficiently many times and {{formula:e34009a3-459d-4311-8835-67d602286076}} for all {{formula:a40e1ba5-3302-4b52-b6a4-63bf31e647b2}} , where {{formula:0ca48523-e3c8-4f8d-895e-9b8fea42b63d}} and {{formula:b0ba0b66-0393-464c-a370-955f1d2f517e}} stands for the standard Euclidean inner product on {{formula:84e6b0ca-ad68-4198-a155-21ef131edb63}} . Consider the unit tangent vector {{formula:9b5ee954-a597-4432-964e-c177ed8c2fcd}} and the unit normal vector {{formula:66608be0-23c5-44a7-bf84-44ac1a183567}} of {{formula:00b3911f-1a32-4c68-b677-47c44ecb178a}} , where {{formula:30a17d05-09f3-4f06-a8e7-2b28d6612a9c}} is the anti-clockwise rotation by {{formula:9910b5dc-f8cb-44db-a542-9a7563e035bc}} . The pair {{formula:62cbf11c-080b-4848-96a4-c744219a8698}} satisfies the Frenet equations {{formula:b8618f1b-8d28-4578-8fac-2f09bb3b22e8}} and {{formula:35f11c4b-fdc6-4e21-93a4-78dbb598b276}} , where {{formula:029d39dd-27ac-4bbe-aef1-ffe96c3ecbaf}} is the curvature of {{formula:a6b67ab2-b7c9-4801-8d2d-8c3fa2eadd80}} . We denote by {{formula:d575f0a6-817e-44df-9124-04b5cf7101d8}} the arc length at {{formula:3580c94e-e6db-48f1-a1ed-cd7dabf69b8a}} of {{formula:ddfb6e3d-8c16-401f-882f-0248ecd7b51f}} with respect to the starting point {{formula:d5f7465f-9772-4fc0-b465-254a268100f9}} .Assume that the curvature {{formula:718f9e1b-ef68-4e7e-94fa-183d4d7116ec}} is a nonvanishing function on {{formula:8b64f357-9c8f-4207-b09e-3b35398cf1bd}} . Let {{formula:dc92c9f8-77df-4cd9-9ba7-0d1eae6e450b}} be the (signed) radius of curvature at {{formula:3cab7b64-00db-448a-993f-805fb8d859a9}} . The evolute of {{formula:5ea167ef-38a7-455b-ba27-e6d8a48cdcaa}} is the curve {{formula:e3f84bd6-8337-4ab8-9742-13e5c7c80f15}} defined by {{formula:63c60d48-91ee-4bfb-9bad-01bfbe587d60}} which is a regular curve if, additionally, {{formula:1c96ca81-3012-49cb-8eae-2ae64dc986a7}} is a nonvanishing function on {{formula:5c58cee6-e71b-4e11-9027-54ebcf5f3627}} . In this case, the curvature {{formula:30b6966d-fd53-4853-b9ae-d3a98e055e1b}} of {{formula:8919bd68-5a58-4c5c-b934-e30a07bf1906}} is given by {{formula:da4d089e-c64a-428f-bfc8-b6f34e69b145}}We also have {{formula:fb1752d2-3294-436e-af07-be3ba9c04c2f}}which means that {{formula:51cfc36f-77c9-498f-87b1-b9a1e4de41a6}} is an arc length parameter of the evolute.If {{formula:9c1e5399-b87e-4943-89a1-ef15960456ea}} is an arc length parameter of {{formula:a422d52c-fc3b-4b4b-addd-e844e105c6b2}} , the curve {{formula:083ce003-79a7-467f-8f60-679a64266ddc}} is an involute of {{formula:050936af-4424-48d8-929d-8a30f936b7a6}} . It is well known that the evolute of the involute {{formula:e285894d-868f-4e0f-9d27-b80ae1a505db}} is precisely {{formula:1291ff76-171c-4b3c-a4dc-3bf0919dafab}} and that, for any other choice of arc length parameter, the corresponding involute of {{formula:06b35990-2d1f-46b5-87f4-bc99e8293f0e}} is parallel to {{formula:7b658337-28c0-424e-88ab-6ceeee708558}} .Finally, recall that, given a smooth function {{formula:27052652-e7eb-4c49-92b1-577c2ea6f7a8}} , there exists a plane curve {{formula:bc3f5f5f-5ed8-4cf4-a697-02be7ec2a812}} parameterized by arc length whose curvature is {{formula:df174a1a-53ab-458c-8501-631787f60e0e}} . Moreover, {{formula:a5fa8192-0d6a-427c-814a-79bb00634ac5}} is unique up to rigid motion and is given by {{formula:79330238-baf2-4d64-8537-7413bdc10bf5}} where the turning angle {{formula:dc1abe60-5b83-4929-a310-153a85417e1e}} is given by {{formula:56464b39-5ece-4313-a46e-60c0fea6c7ac}}
Laguerre geometry and the Minkowski 3-space: Consider on {{formula:b2b28fbe-1b88-459c-bda7-0de559f3d775}} the Lorentzian inner product defined by {{formula:8765ff41-984f-4fb3-972a-a3175b232368}} for {{formula:6ca14117-b474-4102-bbb2-366fe19879e7}} and {{formula:c2fe9fcd-1559-4d28-bb08-c09625d22bf5}} . The Minkowski 3-space is the metric space {{formula:32f0e3bc-fd1b-4739-b12e-e36678d69a45}} . If {{formula:a3a72632-e200-4760-bc85-cab97adb1900}} is a spacelike vector, which means that {{formula:04f39cd6-4f36-460a-9c21-f9d9e955e0e7}} , we denote {{formula:92af0b7f-33f2-4dd7-8d29-04ad8a5cc138}} . The light cone {{formula:a90eca2f-583e-460e-be45-a1146af1ad42}} with vertex at {{formula:bf2bda59-dfda-45e7-ae8e-638e8a11fbef}} is the quadric {{formula:5c085cd2-6717-42d3-9ad6-1052d513de64}}We have a 1-1 correspondence, called the isotropic projection, between points in {{formula:d942daf5-c542-44a8-b8a8-e87dbd1b6936}} and oriented circles in the Euclidean plane, which is defined as follows. Given {{formula:4c69b40b-abfb-4798-b6c4-213cbda0bdde}} in {{formula:43d8088a-e605-48bc-8eca-d9bec8b0c25d}} , consider the light cone {{formula:43cb3c99-807d-46a8-8195-63b8978688a9}} . The intersection of {{formula:32cdbe31-3f00-4f43-8d86-2055d201c553}} with the Euclidean plane {{formula:7ecba45c-43c9-44ec-88ca-c9f56b7be6f9}} is a circle centered at {{formula:9eb24bcc-16ad-40ca-bccb-4cf083e6b4d3}} with radius {{formula:1faafbfe-fccc-480c-bd91-eed7233d35a0}} . The orientation of this circle is anti-clockwise if {{formula:6ec91a2e-471a-489d-be71-35df6cd0add6}} and clockwise if {{formula:6910f575-6f8f-47a9-888b-dc3eaaebb293}} . Points in {{formula:3dde911f-5e8e-47aa-bfd5-02e39a6fcaf5}} are regarded as circles of zero radius and correspond to points {{formula:81567a98-1619-4e98-b303-a4590a7430aa}} in {{formula:d68f7628-3e06-4bf5-924a-451d5c173c9f}} with {{formula:90fbf768-6324-4251-b288-b46850eec13c}} . Making use of this correspondence, Laguerre transformations are precisely those affine transformations {{formula:da6e4779-476c-4c60-83b4-30742c9bd0f5}} of the form {{formula:e71e615e-ef64-4b5d-95f1-76ee954f5730}} , where {{formula:26f09c54-b660-4410-a2a2-de2e81bcd1ca}} , {{formula:4360a6fb-50d5-4481-9d75-65616901d6b9}} and {{formula:708f60d4-87b6-4c95-bb7e-1a5cf52e92c2}} is an orthogonal transformation of {{formula:c3c191d6-4040-4217-8a5b-930bd7ecbea0}} . For details see .
Null curves in Minkowski 3-space: Next we recall some standard facts concerning null curves in the Minkowski 3-space. For details, we refer the reader to , .A regular curve {{formula:428b013b-c18c-4063-92f5-81e0de73f73c}} with parameter {{formula:974cfb03-1505-46db-839f-df4717404aec}} is called a null curve if {{formula:4cdec7c1-6598-4e29-9cfe-5b8666d535de}} is lightlike, that is {{formula:d1e8d02d-f814-4671-8e0b-2b18bec9d61f}} . Differentiating this, we obtain {{formula:074232b2-d744-4be5-bd8a-685ed5e47f44}} , which means that {{formula:f321df26-a5e2-4581-ac94-7b19915b2b47}} lies in {{formula:b4e7d606-2da6-41b0-aa1a-6b2cae7fbcfd}} . We will assume throughout this paper that {{formula:c301c8f8-2190-49af-af33-942a38452d36}} and {{formula:1d7e3682-6c8b-4b94-ba32-13bc2e1e9047}} are linearly independent for all {{formula:19f98430-91b8-45af-a131-2fffb9331d6f}} (in particular, {{formula:f3169bfb-d7bb-465b-b96b-dda6106b078b}} can not be a straight line). answerWithPaperReferences: The Euler equations only admit trivial rotating vortex patches when the angular velocity is Ω = 1/2, as shown in [Paper A]. First 12750 characters: On the trivial solutions for the rotating patch model
abstract: In this paper we study the clockwise simply connected rotating patches for Euler equations. By using the moving plane method we prove that Rankine vortices are the only solutions to this problem in the class of {\it slightly} convex domains. We discuss in the second part of the paper the case where the angular velocity $\Omega=\frac12$ and we show without any geometric condition that the set of the V-states is trivial and reduced to the Rankine vortices.
Introduction: We shall study in this paper some aspects of the vortex motion for the two-dimensional incompressible Euler system which can be written with the vorticity-velocity formulation in the form, {{formula:b71278f7-641d-411d-bf16-2cadfb463c0e}}Here {{formula:c307da8c-93ae-4e5e-bf1b-4909edde40f7}} {{formula:f7b6fa6d-878b-4585-810f-cedf732fafe5}} is the velocity field and the {{formula:316d9bab-84f2-4f3e-80a9-201c375706c8}} its vorticity given by the scalar {{formula:f4f9d2d7-7bf5-4d87-b121-8fe235575f89}} The classical theory dealing with the local{{formula:b7aa6fa4-e5bf-45a9-bf92-e525e75267f9}} global well-posedness of smooth solutions is well developed and we refer for instance to , .According to Yudovich result the vorticity equation has a unique global solution in the weak sense provided the initial vorticity {{formula:c4da050a-3bc6-4707-bffa-4e1ae78789b0}} belongs to {{formula:ca76f893-afec-4509-8d8e-98fd14e93630}} . This result allows to deal rigorously with the so-called vortex patches which are initial vortices uniformly distributed in a confined region {{formula:6dc1886f-0bae-4805-82cc-1a41033e3879}} , that is, {{formula:1ed27a38-782c-44c4-a0db-a0f967ebe420}} the characteristic function of {{formula:9c457e31-2443-4164-9132-8c54ede4160f}} Since the vorticity is transported along trajectories, we conclude that the vorticity preserves the vortex patch structure for any positive time. This means that for any {{formula:fb3cc18b-de21-4632-a7c6-326747c2888e}} , {{formula:1eee5383-4451-4679-af58-d2cd6011b391}} , with {{formula:d57638a2-09dc-4c60-90c3-1f39113412c9}} is the image of {{formula:9e16655e-1ffe-4413-9810-ef4ced25dc56}} by the flow {{formula:41b8d154-359c-42a0-8494-d912e6aaaa50}} which satisfies the ordinary differential equation {{formula:aa5ed63b-91bc-4152-874e-2f3a04b5d534}}The dynamics of the boundary of {{formula:92e88c4c-c894-48bd-bb06-18f1500385e1}} is in general complex and very difficult to follow. By using the contour dynamics method we may parametrize the boundary by a function {{formula:7edd4acc-d08b-4aa6-a760-8568c29c2694}} satisfying a nonlinear and non local equation of the following type {{formula:c94a6228-ad08-4745-a8c9-e743da3d9356}}There are few examples known in the literature with explicit dynamics. The first one is Rankine vortex where {{formula:cf8a453a-6dde-44d8-af71-43ef15e508d0}} is a disc, in this case the particle trajectories are circles centered at the origin, and therefore {{formula:f4c857c8-028a-4c9a-8123-38e9d953b002}} The second example is a remarkable one and discovered by Kirchhoff is the ellipses. In this case the domain {{formula:8e9c60f3-dd46-4232-914b-b154ab59fba2}} does not change its shape and undergoes a perpetual rotation around its barycenter with uniform angular velocity {{formula:d387a04f-37dd-4df8-9934-2c2675ff5829}} related to the semi-axes {{formula:b9e93c8b-f522-4783-afff-6a2f5f22f80d}} and {{formula:89915d72-610c-40ef-a60d-d300081d7cb4}} through the formula {{formula:588f62d8-c466-45da-86c4-6ebd5a032c9c}} See, for instance, .It seems that the ellipses are till now the only explicit example with such properties but wether or not other non trivial implicit rotating patches exist has been discussed in the last few decades from numerical and theoretical point of view. To be more precise about these structures, we say that {{formula:4d2e7e0f-4c60-4e4a-ab69-92392ed712d2}} is a V-state or a rotating patch if there exists a real number {{formula:f8cec79f-f836-44d0-b099-cd4b8126304f}} called the angular velocity such that the support of the vorticity {{formula:22514c7d-8f79-4880-a586-b126bc5d0e1a}} is described by {{formula:7b5db7c7-70ba-4379-83fd-9f0676afa982}}with {{formula:99616276-ec25-4cb9-8f9c-c81c566f6333}} being the planar rotation with center {{formula:c2ea9db0-45a7-4ef1-aacc-29c404cb4cb3}} and angle {{formula:72187dba-d9c6-4b29-b85c-00a7617e54ce}} Deem and Zabusky were the first to reveal numerically the existence of simply connected V-states with the {{formula:70f5bea4-2ec4-4193-b6d4-d3fa2caf8e40}} fold symmetry for the integer {{formula:679d4fcd-0a09-43fa-bb48-762d78cf4cdb}} Recall that a domain {{formula:c97eaf2c-5135-4ee1-9a8a-18fc6e00361e}} is said to be {{formula:71f6d94a-ee9e-40f0-a6e8-5bd5ec170f40}} -fold symmetric if it is invariant by the dihedral group {{formula:4aaba543-4347-4b8e-b2af-f3fcdbca91ef}} which is the symmetry group of a regular polygon of {{formula:3228cc75-66c7-468f-a13b-cc13928e32c0}} sides. A few years later, Burbea gave an analytic proof by using the bifurcation theory showing the existence of a countable family of V-states with the {{formula:1fad6c66-e465-4def-8335-d1416871588a}} -fold symmetry for any {{formula:bbbad1b2-fee0-49c3-854f-666cc211d90b}} . They can be identified to one-dimensional branches bifurcating from the Rankine vortex at the simple “eigenvalues" {{formula:c9bd5fd8-5f88-4485-b3df-48d57e545817}} See also , where the {{formula:0799c4e5-fe2e-4383-a11a-7c96d6ac0942}} boundary regularity of the bifurcated {{formula:ec9e0710-9950-4f71-a63e-be07efcffccb}} states close to the disc was proven. It seems that close to the disc, the bifurcating branches rotate with bounded angular velocities, {{formula:582dd708-045d-43ef-b2bf-7c087278a978}} . It is important to know wether all the V-states possess an angular velocity in this strip. First 12971 characters: Vortex rigid motion in quasi-geostrophic shallow-water equations
abstract: In this paper, we prove the existence of relative equilibria with holes for quasi-geostrophic shallow-water equations. More precisely, using bifurcation techniques, we establish for any m large enough the existence of two branches of m-fold doubly-connected V-states bifurcating from any annulus of arbitrary size.
QGSW equations and main result: In this work, we are concerned with the quasi-geostrophic shallow-water equations with a parameter {{formula:a0fc19f0-7554-4b11-b0a3-8131f39d8c66}} , which is a two dimensional active scalar equation taking the form {{formula:c41fa57f-36e3-420a-92e6-0de02b52be52}}The involved quantities are the divergence-free velocity field {{formula:f25a068e-29e7-495a-9cc5-759fa1180c1b}} and the potential vorticity {{formula:e4703ea1-e93d-4e55-bb74-2f8e8c1db551}} which is a scalar function. The parameter {{formula:bb6296e7-3961-440f-865e-6929cc0e8079}} stands for the inverse Rossby radius defined in the literature by {{formula:061e97d7-63ea-4da5-8ccd-c532b733bda8}}where {{formula:283153d6-a8db-40ac-87be-e0f9eeb238a6}} is the gravity constant, {{formula:cd12135c-3b5b-46b5-a89f-b68e443c2c4f}} is the mean active layer depth and {{formula:b540bf31-db6d-43d1-83d9-fd689c5a4ace}} is the Coriolis frequency, assumed to be constant. Notice that the case {{formula:a7440751-fc85-483a-9b06-e6783c86c13c}} corresponds to the velocity-vorticity formulation of Euler equations. The system (REF ) is commonly used to track the dynamics of the atmospheric and oceanic circulation at large scale motion. For a general review about the asymptotic derivation of the these equations from the rotating shallow water equations we refer for instance to .The main purpose of this paper is to explore the emergence of time periodic solutions in the patch form close to the annulus of radii 1 and {{formula:d8d9dbfa-b578-4a03-b435-624ec029e10d}} for the system {{formula:f60b8efc-a25c-4e44-8d43-a953b4333f98}} with fixed {{formula:7eba0982-9ecc-4303-aec1-5b677da86b27}} and {{formula:a1ddea8d-a730-4f58-984a-a45416544bff}} Recall that a vortex patch means a solution of (REF ) with initial condition being the characteristic function of a bounded domain {{formula:6551b7a0-36cb-465b-9b36-1422f18f6e5d}} , that is {{formula:d1844563-9874-434d-9a49-ebba2946886f}} Actually, this structure is conserved in time due to the transport structure of (REF ), and one gets {{formula:ab05e079-dd28-49c7-ac48-f5f846b6f626}}with {{formula:4759fb0d-fb13-469d-8e8e-046df1014010}} is the flow map associated to {{formula:5048327f-24d7-453b-bfa6-eea084772199}} , defined through the ODE {{formula:ef7bdd70-f969-475b-a393-7d88b65a6dce}}In this framework, of bounded datum with compact support, existence and uniqueness follow in a standard way from Yudovich approach implemented for Euler equations and which can be adapted here in a similar way. These structures can be considered as a toy model to simulate hurricanes motion in the context of geophysical flows. In the smooth boundary case, their dynamics is completely described by the evolution of the interfaces surrounding the patch according to the contour dynamics equation given by {{formula:305b8ce1-dfcf-48d8-a180-558f8d613c15}}where {{formula:3cae46dc-6ce8-4fa8-bc99-ebbd9d39f6a4}} is a {{formula:2d7d8a2a-b8f9-45c2-b725-30872ed9f433}} parametrization of the boundary of the patch and {{formula:c0962c4c-e6db-4df0-ab01-6946329d2400}} is an outward normal vector to the boundary. We may refer to , for a detailed derivation of this equation for active scalar models. We are particularly interested in the existence of ordered structures moving without shape deformation, called V-states. More precisely, we shall focus on the existence of uniformly rotating vortex patches about their center of mass, that can be fixed at the origin, and with a constant angular velocity {{formula:400b5cb1-3f94-4422-b0cd-92841d82fc12}} , namely {{formula:8a0639b4-dd55-428b-a86f-8d5bbe0b3330}}In the present work we explore the case of doubly-connected V-states with {{formula:ca531d4d-a656-4bd5-af7a-fec9baba6772}} -fold symmetry. To fix the terminology, a bounded open domain {{formula:7e80b311-0e12-4bcd-b0f3-7efb95ac8793}} is said doubly-connected if {{formula:66d19a26-e775-4c01-8cd3-90d1b262a350}}where {{formula:41dc8330-b888-4e53-aeb3-1b09daaf9e62}} and {{formula:96739925-e797-4035-b34c-8f083c6610f7}} are two bounded open simply-connected domains with {{formula:f03647de-e716-4440-ab93-1d7db96b7b48}} This means that the boundary of {{formula:a50774fe-63a8-4c1b-b07c-9206ffac76f7}} is given by two interfaces, one of them is contained in the open region delimited by the second one. According to the structure of {{formula:bb0d4187-1a2c-4a2a-928c-2ba7b701ab2f}} , every radial initial domain {{formula:dcd47a6c-ed97-4b22-b256-031120ba168a}} generates a trivial stationary solution, and therefore a V-state rotating with any angular velocity. Basic examples are given by the discs in the simply-connected case or the annuli in the doubly-connected case. The first non-trivial examples of uniformly rotating solutions for Euler equations are Kirchhoff ellipses which rotate with the angular velocity {{formula:3c0c00a6-9dc2-4444-a815-6ff539ba5f1a}} where {{formula:c0de6106-15b7-4431-bc5b-ab253d9e7533}} and {{formula:a69c74bf-9e95-4ec8-8443-cb91fb81c366}} are the semi-axes of the ellipse (see and ). In Deem and Zabusky established numerically the existence of simply-connected rotating patches with {{formula:fef8d504-976d-4868-8af3-a53a23dee527}} -fold symmetry for {{formula:f6d55009-72b9-490b-aae7-bb215e520bec}} An analytical proof based on bifurcation theory and complex analysis tools was performed by Burbea in showing the existence of {{formula:b3bd4e6a-5a18-48d1-922f-20ddafb6a7f7}} -fold (for any {{formula:56b26626-0e98-4f79-9e58-298f213269b2}} ) symmetric V-states bifurcating from Rankine vortices with angular velocity {{formula:32083697-d5f2-4dd4-b66d-71a720fe29e6}} . In the spirit of Burbea's work, a lot of results on {{formula:a17627f3-d0fe-43d0-86fd-5ba4cca1bd4d}} -fold V-states have been obtained both for simply and doubly-connected cases for Euler, {{formula:44df0d7b-da90-4fa4-b659-080f5e62eaf1}} and {{formula:2dfec056-f9d3-421c-b518-e09ec6fea9ff}} equations in the past decade. We may refer to , , , , , , , . From this long list, we shall make some comments on two contributions from , related to the current work. In , the authors proved for Euler equations that under the condition {{formula:ba7c3900-5abe-45cd-af38-bb45bc82b877}}one can find two branches of {{formula:9eae9b5c-d3a7-40a9-a5a0-07596ab0b7c6}} -fold doubly-connected V-states bifurcating from the normalized annulus {{formula:98ad6d56-bbb7-4020-b800-8a64bfc961ce}} , defined by {{formula:d1f7c443-1cc0-4ab9-b99f-a7e2a987bb78}}at the following angular velocities {{formula:7d918a0b-c410-49a4-88d0-e75aaf9b019e}}Burbea's result has been extended for {{formula:666b49b9-e880-45fb-8a81-2ecbb420bd18}} in , where it is shown the existence of branches of {{formula:a9cc3a85-7601-4678-bc6e-dd07e7b1d0b7}} -fold symmetric V-states ({{formula:2a4d783e-5458-4c36-ad27-e118d6730b24}} ) bifurcating from Rankine vortex {{formula:7b6dad67-2f98-4147-a380-22cbf1232db3}} , with {{formula:91fb124d-c8ef-4c85-816e-fca2a37167de}} being the unit disc, at the angular velocitity {{formula:9f26f9aa-fd0a-4b3b-86c5-c2bfcde1c979}}where {{formula:9157fa6f-ec69-414f-b8e4-84b7f39a0eee}} and {{formula:b646f384-3630-4c56-be81-915c1dafaf00}} are the modified Bessel functions of first and second kind, respectively. We may refer to the Appendix for the definitions and some basic properties of these functions. We also notice that more analytical and numerical experiments were carefully explored in , dealing in particular with the imperfect bifurcation and the response of the bifurcation diagram with respect to the parameter {{formula:f7d48f4d-cf82-4dec-b416-810a6c16841c}}We emphasize that different studies around this subject have been recently investigated by several authors, we refer for instance to , , , , , and the references therein.The main contribution of this paper is to establish for {{formula:4f811a65-7191-49e6-ba80-66698fe27471}} the existence of branches of bifurcation in the doubly-connected case, generalizing the result of . More precisely, we prove the following result.Theorem 1.1 Let {{formula:de7141b8-977c-440d-b4de-5408bd7f4248}} and {{formula:c6fcd723-03b0-4731-ab56-f6ad80780c37}} . reasoning.step1: Paper A (1502.01852) derives the MSRA initialization method specifically for deep rectifier networks (ReLU/PReLU). It theoretically justifies scaling initial weights to account for rectifier nonlinearities, enabling stable training of very deep models by maintaining the variance of layer responses.
reasoning.step2: Paper B (1903.02240) empirically evaluates MSRA initialization when training their lightweight Photo-realistic Cascading Residual Network (PCARN) for super-resolution. They observe that MSRA initialization performs poorly because PCARN uses considerably fewer channels than ResNet and employs narrow 1×1 convolutions (with only one-ninth the input channels of 3×3 layers), causing high-variance initial values that lead to unstable training. They instead require an initialization with smaller variance to avoid premature convergence.
reasoning.connectionExplanation: Step 2 directly depends on Step 1 because Paper B explicitly tests the MSRA method introduced in Paper A and explains its failure by contrasting PCARN's narrow, lightweight architecture against the deeper, wider ResNet-style architectures for which MSRA was originally derived. Without Paper A, one would lack the theoretical basis and intended use case of MSRA initialization; without Paper B, one would not know that this initialization fails for lightweight super-resolution networks with narrow 1×1 convolutions or what alternative is needed.

questionDraft: Why does the MSRA initialization method, which was designed for rectifier networks, perform poorly when training a lightweight cascading residual super-resolution network with narrow 1×1 convolutions, and what alternative initialization property is needed?
question: Why does the initialization method designed for rectifier networks with ReLU or PReLU activations perform poorly when applied to a lightweight cascading residual network for image super-resolution that uses narrow 1×1 convolutions, and what alternative initialization property is required to ensure stable training?
answerWithPaperReferences: The MSRA initialization method [Paper A] was derived specifically for rectifier networks (ReLU and PReLU) to maintain the variance of responses across deep layers by scaling initial weights according to the nonlinearity of rectifiers. However, when applied to the lightweight super-resolution network PCARN [Paper B], this initialization performs poorly because the model employs considerably fewer channels than typical ResNet architectures and relies heavily on narrow 1×1 convolutions that have only one-ninth of the input channels compared to 3×3 layers. These architectural choices cause the high-variance MSRA initialization to produce unstable initial values, leading to high-variance performance. Consequently, PCARN requires an initialization with a much smaller variance—one whose distribution better matches the narrower channel dimensions—to avoid premature convergence and achieve stable training.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: The initialization method designed for rectifier networks scales initial weights to account for ReLU or PReLU nonlinearities and maintain variance across deep layers. However, when training a lightweight cascading residual network for image super-resolution with narrow 1×1 convolutions and significantly fewer channels than standard recognition networks, this initialization produces high-variance initial values that destabilize training. Because the 1×1 convolutions use only one-ninth of the input channels compared to 3×3 layers, the high-variance initialization leads to erratic performance. Therefore, such lightweight super-resolution networks require an initialization scheme with substantially smaller variance to prevent premature convergence and ensure stable optimization.
isNotSingleHop: The question is not single-hop because Paper A provides the theoretical derivation and intended use case of MSRA initialization for rectifier networks, while Paper B provides the specific architectural constraints (narrow 1×1 convolutions, few channels) that cause it to fail and the empirical finding about the required alternative. Neither paper alone contains both the derivation of MSRA initialization and its failure mode in super-resolution networks, nor does either paper alone explain why the method fails in this specific architectural context and what property is needed instead.
